# Writing is a skill

Academic work involves a great deal of writing: papers, grant proposals,
application materials, software documentation, dissertation chapters. All of it
can be learned and improved like any other skill --- calculus, programming,
gardening. It is also hard, especially if you care about quality, and it is
mostly a matter of **discipline** rather than talent.

Four practices do most of the work:

- **Plan regular time blocks**, even short ones. Thirty minutes on a schedule
  beats waiting for a long stretch.
- **Separate generating text from editing.** Generating is about 20% of writing;
  editing is the other 80%. Doing both at once stalls you on the first sentence.
- **Embrace the bad first draft.** Its only job is to exist. You cannot edit a
  blank page.
- **Plan for repeated feedback**, and expect to edit, edit, edit as a result.

What not to do:

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| Write one sentence and rewrite it five times | Editing before there is anything to edit |
| Wait for a free three-hour block | It rarely comes; short blocks accumulate |
| Wait for inspiration | Writing is discipline, not mood |
| Give up because you are "not good at it" | It is a skill, and skills respond to practice |
| Polish grammar before asking for feedback | Wasted effort on text that may be cut |

: Habits that keep people from finishing {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

Excellence has two halves. The **process**: dedicated time and focus, generation
separated from editing, planned feedback and multiple rounds of edits, version
control (Overleaf for LaTeX, Google Docs for Word). The **product**: it follows
the expected structure with all required components; its style is tailored to the
audience; it aims to educate rather than confuse, with clear word choices and
simple sentences and no hidden steps; and it is concise and concrete --- no
watery sentences, no filler, claims substantiated with references.

# Structure

Two structures cover most cases. Decide the target journal first, then find two
or three example papers from it to guide structure, style, and language.

| Statistical methodology journals | Life sciences / domain journals |
|---|---|
| Introduction | Introduction |
| Methods (may be several sections) | Methods |
| Simulation studies | Results |
| Application to X study | Discussion (often long) |
| Discussion / Conclusions | |

: Two common paper structures

Machine learning conference papers usually merge simulation and data analysis
into a single Numerical Comparison section, since benchmark datasets are standard
there rather than simulated data.

What each section does:

**Methods** describes what you are going to do and how --- *not* the results. In
a domain paper: study design (data source, collection, what was collected), data
processing, statistical methods. In a methods paper: study design and processing
if relevant, then the proposed model and estimation procedure (the core), then
theoretical investigation if applicable.

**Results** presents findings without interpreting them. In a domain paper: Table
1 with sample characteristics, exploratory analysis as applicable, then results
from fitted models. In a methods paper this is two sections --- Simulation
studies, which always covers data generation, methods for comparison, metrics for
comparison, and results; and Application to X study, which covers study design
and processing (if not given earlier), methods for comparison including the
proposed one, and results.

**Discussion** gives a two-to-three sentence summary, then strengths and
limitations, then opportunities for future research. Domain papers discuss at
length, especially limitations and scientific implications. Statistics papers are
shorter --- often a single paragraph, focused on the method and on future
improvements.

**Abstract**, typically 250 words or fewer, mirrors the paper: introduction,
methods, results, conclusion. It must be self-contained, so that a reader gets
the idea of the paper without reading it.

# The introduction

The introduction moves from broad to narrow and must hit four things: the context
of the problem and why anyone should care; existing approaches and why they fall
short (or what gaps remain in what is known); the new thing you will do about it;
and an explicit statement of the work's contributions.

Paragraph by paragraph, a typical version:

| Paragraph | Job |
|---|---|
| 1 | Context for the problem. For a data-centric paper, connect to the data immediately. Establish that this is a setting worth looking at. |
| 2–3 | Literature review: what has been done. The punchline is the gap or the limitation. |
| 4 | Motivate your approach from that gap. The big sell --- what is cool about it, how it overcomes the limitation. |
| Last | Outline of the paper: "The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we…" --- one line per section. |

: The arc of a typical introduction {tbl-colwidths="[14,86]"}

> Journals differ on that last paragraph. Most expect it; a few explicitly ask
> that it be left out. Check before you submit.

Real introductions vary around this template, and reading several of your target
journal's is the fastest way to calibrate. A theoretical paper may go straight to
a mathematical statement of the problem and close with a point-by-point
contributions list. A short computational paper may spend two paragraphs on why
the problem matters, one on the limitation of the state of the art, and one on
how it is solved. An applied paper may open with the data type and concrete data
questions before reviewing methods at all.

# Why papers get rejected

Most rejections trace to one of six reader reactions. Each has a fix, and each
fix belongs mostly in the introduction.

| The reader… | What addresses it |
|---|---|
| doesn't think the work is novel | Acknowledge existing work properly, and say clearly how yours differs and what is new |
| doesn't see the problem being addressed | Articulate the specific question or problem the work solves |
| sees the problem but doesn't think it matters | Connect to the scientific domain through consequences --- if this is not addressed, then what? |
| doesn't understand what you did, or why it solves the problem | State contributions explicitly, contrast with prior work, present results so they visibly solve the problem |
| doesn't think it fits the audience | Ask who cares most, whether it matches the journal's aims and scope, and whether it is written for that reader |
| finds the work sloppy | Feedback, multiple edits, proofreading |

: Six reasons, and what fixes them {tbl-colwidths="[36,64]"}

# Feedback checklist {.unnumbered}

Give this to a reader --- and use it on yourself. After reading only the abstract
and introduction, they should be able to check every box:

- [ ] I clearly understand the problem the work addresses, or the knowledge gap it fills
- [ ] I clearly see why addressing this problem is important
- [ ] I understand the approach the authors took
- [ ] I am convinced the approach differs from what has been tried, in meaningful ways
- [ ] I am convinced the approach succeeds in addressing the problem
- [ ] I found the writing easy to follow, and I learned something from reading it

# Practical notes {.unnumbered}

**Find model papers.** Identify the target venue first, then look through recent
issues for two or three well-written accepted papers resembling yours. Use them
to judge how introductions are written, what goes in the discussion, and how much
detail belongs in the main body versus the appendix. Ask a senior author whether
the ones you picked are good guides.

**Write in active present voice.** *We consider…*, *we apply our method to…*,
*we compare…*; likewise *Figure 1 shows*, *Table 1 shows*. The exception is a
domain journal whose field prefers the passive.

**Use the LaTeX template.** The lab's LaTeX template document covers labels and
cross-referencing, mathematical notation conventions, bibliography management
with BibTeX, and tables, figures, and algorithms. Two rules from it worth
repeating here: generate LaTeX tables from R with `xtable` rather than copying
numbers by hand, and save figures with the `pdf()` command rather than the
RStudio export button.

**Get help.** The [SPH Writing Lab](https://sph.umich.edu/writing-lab/) and the
[Sweetland Center for Writing](https://lsa.umich.edu/sweetland/undergraduates/writing-support.html)
both offer support.

# Further reading {.unnumbered}

Strunk W, White EB. *The Elements of Style* --- grammar and style.

Silvia PJ. *How to Write a Lot: A Practical Guide to Productive Academic
Writing*. APA LifeTools --- motivation and persistence.

Goodson P. *Becoming an Academic Writer: 50 Exercises for Paced, Productive, and
Powerful Writing*. SAGE --- exercises, and advice on specific sections.

Lamott A (1994). *Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life*. Anchor
Books --- the chapter on first drafts is the classic statement of why bad first
drafts are the only route to good final ones. See also the Publication Coach's
["The joy of the crappy first draft"](https://www.publicationcoach.com/crappy-first-draft/).

Ecarnot F, Seronde M-F, Chopard R, Schiele F, Meneveau N (2015). Writing a
scientific article: a step-by-step guide for beginners. *European Geriatric
Medicine*, 6(6), 573--579 --- a practical walkthrough aimed at first-time
authors.
